1023.title: The caliphate ends, 1924
1023.hook: the Ottoman caliphate is abolished by the new Turkish Republic
1023.howItsDone: Muslims today organize religious life through mosques, scholars, councils and national religious bodies, and they hold differing views about whether and how a caliphate should exist.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Iqbal, the poet of khudi. Your line was the self can rise. Today, something very old comes to a stop.

The new parliament of the Turkish Republic has voted, and an office no longer exists. That night in Istanbul, the man who held it is told he must leave the country. He paints and plays music, and his title, as tradition tells it, reaches back to the first generation after the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Before dawn he and his family are taken to a train west, into Europe. He will not come back. In India, Egypt and Indonesia, Muslims read the news. Some weep. Some shrug. Some start organizing to bring it back. Today: the caliphate ends.
screen: `THE PARLIAMENT HAS VOTED.` → `A PAINTER WITH AN ANCIENT TITLE.` → `A TRAIN WEST, BEFORE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Caliph comes from the Arabic khalifa, a successor or deputy. After the Prophet's death, Sunni Muslims hold, the community chose Abu Bakr as successor; Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet had named Ali. The title passed down, through dynasties and quarrels, until it rested with the Ottoman sultans. The same root reaches back into the Qur'an. In Pickthall's words, when God tells the angels about Adam: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." A khalifa. How much real power the caliph held changed a great deal: sometimes an empire, sometimes mostly a symbol. After the Ottoman Empire fell apart following the First World War, the new parliament in Ankara first ended the sultanate, kept a caliph without a throne for a short while, and then, once the Republic was declared, abolished the office entirely. The last caliph, Abdulmecid, went into exile. How did Muslims take it? Not in one way. In India, a movement that had campaigned hard to protect the caliphate lost its cause overnight. Some scholars gathered to talk about naming a new caliph, and nothing came of it. Others said a Muslim's faith had never depended on one office in Istanbul. Today Muslims still differ: some hope to see a caliphate again, others organize their religious life through mosques, scholars and councils, and they argue about it openly. The Qur'an says of power, in Pickthall's words: "Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt, and Thou withdrawest sovereignty from whom Thou wilt." An institution ends. Prayer goes on.
screen: `KHALIFA: A SUCCESSOR, A DEPUTY.` · `FROM EMPIRE TO SYMBOL.` · `THE REPUBLIC ABOLISHES THE OFFICE.` · `MUSLIMS ANSWER IN MANY WAYS.` · then, large: `THOU WITHDRAWEST SOVEREIGNTY FROM WHOM THOU WILT.`

Notice what it held for people, and who picked up that work when it was gone, if anyone did. If you pray, hold Qur'an 3:26 in mind, that sovereignty is given and withdrawn.

Your line: an institution ends. Offices pass; the questions they raise stay. Day one thousand twenty-three.

1024.title: Partition, 1947
1024.hook: India and Pakistan divide, millions are displaced and many killed on all sides
1024.howItsDone: Families in Pakistan, India and Bangladesh pass down Partition memories, and Muslims, like their neighbors, remember those who died with prayers and with the words of Qur'an 2:156 said at any loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the caliphate ended, an office voted out of existence and a caliph sent west on a train. Your line was an institution ends. Today is a heavy day. Go gently.

A key. An old iron house key, kept in a drawer in Lahore, or Delhi, or Amritsar, or Dhaka. The family that keeps it hasn't seen the door it opens for generations. The grandmother who carried it out locked the house behind her, sure she'd be back in a few weeks, once things calmed down. Families on both sides of a new border keep keys like this. Hindu families, Sikh families, Muslim families. The same drawer, the same key, the same door they never opened again. Today: Partition.
screen: `AN OLD IRON KEY IN A DRAWER.` → `SURE SHE'D BE BACK IN A FEW WEEKS.` → `THE SAME KEY ON BOTH SIDES.`

segments.voice: When British rule in India ended, the land was divided into two states, India and Pakistan, with Pakistan itself in two wings, west and east. A British commission drew the line in a hurry, through the provinces of Punjab and Bengal, through farms and villages and families. Some people learned which country they lived in only after independence had already come. Then came the leaving. Muslims moving toward Pakistan. Hindus and Sikhs moving toward India. On foot, in carts, on overcrowded trains. And then the killing, done by people of every community to people of every community, neighbors turned against neighbors. Women suffered terribly. Accounts tell of trains that arrived carrying only the dead. An honest telling says it plainly: cruelty on all sides, and grief on all sides. And there's the other thread. The oral histories gathered since include people who hid a neighbor of another faith in a grain store, walked a family to safety, refused to give up a name. Hindus sheltering Muslims. Muslims sheltering Sikhs. Sikhs sheltering Hindus. The Qur'an sets the weight of one life in a single sentence. In Pickthall's words: "whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind." And at any loss, Muslims say the words of surah al-Baqarah: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." That summer, some had nothing else left to say. Grief on every side.
screen: `A LINE DRAWN IN A HURRY.` · `THE LEAVING, THEN THE KILLING.` · `NEIGHBORS WHO HID NEIGHBORS.` · `THE WEIGHT OF ONE LIFE.` · then, large: `UNTO HIM WE ARE RETURNING.`

Don't sort them into sides; just hold them, all together. If you pray, you can pray for all who were uprooted and say the words Muslims say at a loss, we are Allah's, and unto Him we are returning; if not, just remember them as you breathe.
Partition. The division of British India into India and Pakistan, a leaving and a killing that left grief in every community. Today's word.
Your line: grief on every side. And on every side, someone who hid a neighbor. Gently, until tomorrow.

1025.title: Independence movements
1025.hook: from Indonesia to Algeria, Muslim-majority lands gain independence, often at great cost
1025.howItsDone: Muslim-majority countries mark their independence days with flags, speeches and remembrance of those who died, and in some of them prayers for the nation are offered in mosques on that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Partition, and the key kept in a drawer on both sides of the border. Your line was grief on every side. Today, the long walk out from under empire.

A few typed sentences, read aloud in front of a house in Jakarta to a small crowd. Two men put their names to it: Sukarno and Hatta. It says, plainly, that the people of Indonesia declare their independence. That's it. No army behind it strong enough to hold it yet. The Dutch didn't accept those sentences, and years of fighting and talks followed before they did. Across the Muslim world, the same story played out in many forms: a declaration, a cost, a flag. Today: independence movements.
screen: `A TYPED STATEMENT IN JAKARTA.` → `READ ALOUD TO A SMALL CROWD.` → `YEARS BEFORE IT HELD.`

segments.voice: Arabic has a word for it: istiqlal, independence. In Jakarta, the great national mosque was given that name: the Istiqlal Mosque, the Independence Mosque. A house of prayer named for a political freedom, the two tied together. Faith fed these movements in different ways. In Algeria, under French rule, the scholar Abdelhamid Ben Badis and his association of Muslim scholars opened schools to teach Arabic and the Qur'an, and a motto attributed to him put it in three short lines: Islam is my religion, Arabic is my language, Algeria is my homeland. When Algeria's war of independence came, it was long and terribly costly, on every side, and the scars are still being talked through on both shores of the Mediterranean. Not every road was war. Some lands won independence mostly through negotiation and politics, some through uprising, others through a mix of both. And some of the leaders weren't religious figures at all. Muslims of every kind, devout, secular and in between, marched under the same flags, alongside Christian, Hindu and other neighbors. Some readers turn here to a line of the Qur'an about peoples and nations. In Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Nations, in this verse, are made so that they may know one another. Freedom at a cost.

Independence movements. The struggles that brought Muslim-majority lands out from under empire, through talks, through war, and often at great cost. Today's word.
Your line: freedom at a cost. A flag goes up, and someone paid for it. That's one thousand twenty-five days.

1026.title: Enslaved African Muslims
1026.hook: many enslaved Africans brought to the Americas were Muslim, like Omar ibn Said, who wrote in Arabic
1026.howItsDone: Muslim communities in the Americas, especially African American Muslims, remember enslaved Muslims like Omar ibn Said and Bilali Muhammad in study circles, lectures and museum visits, and some mosques are named in their honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: independence movements, istiqlal, won through talks and war. Your line was freedom at a cost. Today, people with no freedom at all, who kept their prayers anyway.

Marks on the wall of a small jail in North Carolina. A runaway has been locked up, a stranger who speaks no English anyone can follow. On his cell wall are lines of flowing script in charcoal that nobody can read. Townspeople come to stare. The man is a scholar from West Africa, and the script is Arabic. He has been carried across an ocean, sold, and has run from a cruel master, and still he writes. His name is Omar ibn Said, and his story opens a chapter of American history that is easy to miss. Today: enslaved African Muslims.
screen: `A STRANGER IN A CAROLINA JAIL.` → `FLOWING SCRIPT ON THE WALL.` → `A SCHOLAR FROM WEST AFRICA.`

segments.voice: Among the Africans carried across the Atlantic in the slave trade were Muslims. Some were scholars, teachers and pilgrims, people who could read and write Arabic, had memorized long stretches of the Qur'an, and kept the daily prayers. They arrived in chains in the Caribbean, Brazil and the American South, and their enslavers often had no idea what the marks on a scrap of paper meant. Omar ibn Said came from Futa Toro in West Africa, where he had studied for years. In America he was enslaved, ran away, was jailed, and was then held by a family in North Carolina for the rest of his life. Years later he wrote a short account of himself, in Arabic. How does he begin? Not with his own name. After calling on the name of God, he writes out a surah of the Qur'an, al-Mulk, the Dominion. Its first line, in Pickthall's words: "Blessed is He in Whose hand is the Sovereignty, and, He is Able to do all things." Consider who is writing: a man owned by another man, opening his life story by saying that the true sovereignty belongs to God. His enslavers later presented him as a Christian convert, and he did write Christian texts too. But he kept writing the Qur'an's words, and scholars still debate what he believed in his own heart. On the Georgia coast, another enslaved Muslim, Bilali Muhammad, left pages of Arabic writing on prayer and law. Men like these wrote Arabic from memory, far from any teacher, and kept the times of prayer. They prayed in chains.
screen: `MUSLIMS IN THE SLAVE SHIPS.` · `OMAR IBN SAID OF FUTA TORO.` · `HIS STORY OPENS WITH AL-MULK.` · `WHAT HE BELIEVED: STILL DEBATED.` · then, large: `IN WHOSE HAND IS THE SOVEREIGNTY.`

Al-Mulk, the surah on God's sovereignty that Omar ibn Said wrote out from memory to open his own account of an enslaved life. Today's word.

1027.title: Muslims in Britain
1027.hook: a dome in Woking, a terraced house in Liverpool, sailors by the docks in Cardiff
1027.howItsDone: British Muslims pray in a wide range of buildings, from purpose-built mosques to converted houses, shops and chapels, and some local mosques keep and share the history of the people who founded them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: enslaved African Muslims, like Omar ibn Said, who opened his own account with al-Mulk. Your line was they prayed in chains.

A domed mosque sits behind the trees in Woking, a quiet commuter town south of London. It's named for a woman far away, Shah Jahan, the Begum of Bhopal in India, who helped pay for it. Up north in Liverpool, a local solicitor named William Quilliam becomes Muslim, takes the name Abdullah, and opens a mosque in a row of ordinary terraced houses. Down in Cardiff, near the docks, sailors from Yemen and Somalia rent rooms, marry, raise children, and set aside a room to pray. No palace in any of it. Just streets, rain and neighbors. Today: Muslims in Britain.
screen: `A DOME IN WOKING.` → `A TERRACED HOUSE IN LIVERPOOL.` → `SAILORS BY THE CARDIFF DOCKS.`

segments.voice: One idea for today: Muslims in Britain are not a single arrival. They are many threads, woven over a long time. Some are converts, like Abdullah Quilliam in Liverpool. Some are sailors and dock workers, from Yemen, Somalia and the Indian subcontinent, who settled in port towns. Some are soldiers from India who fought in Britain's wars; near that mosque in Woking there is a burial ground made for Muslim soldiers. And then came families, from Pakistan, Bangladesh, India and later from Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans, who came to work in mills, factories, hospitals and buses, and stayed. You can read that history in the buildings. Some mosques were built from the ground up with domes and minarets. Others began as a front room, a shop, a warehouse or an old chapel. On Brick Lane in East London stands a building put up as a chapel for French Protestant refugees, later a synagogue for Jewish families, and now a mosque. One building, three faiths, each praying in turn under the same roof. The Qur'an has a line that fits a faith carried to a cold, rainy island: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." For British Muslims, that has meant praying in a Cardiff boarding house, a Bradford mill, a Woking garden. The faith didn't wait for the perfect place. It found a corner, faced Mecca, and began.
screen: `NOT ONE ARRIVAL, MANY THREADS.` · `CONVERTS, SAILORS, SOLDIERS, FAMILIES.` · `ONE BUILDING, THREE FAITHS.` · `EAST AND WEST BELONG TO GOD.` · then, large: `A LONG BRITISH STORY.`

Then think of the first handful of people who unrolled their prayer mats in that place. If you pray, ask God's mercy for them in your own words; if not, simply hold them in mind.

1028.title: Muslims in America
1028.hook: immigrants, converts and African American Muslims, a very diverse community
1028.howItsDone: American Muslims gather in mosques and Islamic centers founded by immigrant, African American and convert communities, and many mosques hold open houses where neighbors can visit and ask questions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Muslims in Britain, from a dome in Woking to Abdullah Quilliam's terraced houses in Liverpool. Your line was a long british story.

Friday, just after noon, in a mosque in an American city. A man in a Detroit auto plant jacket. A doctor whose parents came from Lahore. A grandmother whose family has been Black and Muslim in Philadelphia for generations. A young woman from a Lutheran family in Minnesota who became Muslim in college. A Somali taxi driver. A Bosnian baker. They stand in one row, and nobody needs to ask where anyone is really from. The answer, for all of them, is here. Today: Muslims in America.
screen: `FRIDAY, JUST AFTER NOON.` → `DETROIT, LAHORE, PHILADELPHIA, MINNESOTA.` → `WHERE ARE YOU FROM? HERE.`

segments.voice: American Muslims are a very varied community, and three big streams run into it. The first is immigrants. Arab families settled in the Midwest and worked in factories; South Asians came as doctors, engineers and students; later came people from Iran, Turkey, Bosnia, Somalia and many other places. The second is African American Muslims. Two days ago we met enslaved Africans who prayed in chains. Slavery made that faith hard to hand down. Later, Black Americans found their way to Islam again, through several movements. Some passed through the Nation of Islam, and under Warith Deen Mohammed much of that community turned to mainstream Sunni practice. The third stream is converts of every background, who walked into a mosque one day and said the shahada. Here's the idea worth keeping. For the people in that Friday row, American and Muslim are not two halves pulling apart. They are one life. The boxer Muhammad Ali took the name, prayed, fought, joked, and was American to his fingertips. The Qur'an says plainly: "There is no compulsion in religion." In America that line can be heard twice: as a teaching of the faith, and as something close to the country's own promise that belief is free. A convert chooses. An immigrant family chooses to stay. A grandchild of the old streams chooses to keep praying.

1029.title: Malcolm X at Hajj
1029.hook: he writes home from Mecca of pilgrims of every color in one brotherhood
1029.howItsDone: Pilgrims on Hajj wear the same simple white garments, pray in shared rows and travel the same route together, and many Muslims speak of the pilgrimage as a lesson in the equality of believers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Muslims in America, immigrants, African American Muslims and converts, three streams in one community. Your line was american and muslim. Today, one American Muslim's story.

A tall American in two plain white cloths, the pilgrim's dress, sits down to write a letter home. For years he has been the fiery voice of a movement in America, speaking hard words about race. Now he is in Mecca, and something in him is shifting. He has walked around the Ka'ba in a crowd from every part of the world. He has eaten from the same plate and slept on the same floor as men whose skin, he writes, ranged from the palest to the darkest. He says he has never seen anything like it. Today: Malcolm X at Hajj.
screen: `TWO WHITE CLOTHS.` → `A LETTER HOME FROM MECCA.` → `THE SAME PLATE, THE SAME FLOOR.`

segments.voice: The man was Malcolm X, and his autobiography gives a chapter to the pilgrimage and the letters he wrote from it. He describes praying, eating and sleeping beside pilgrims of every color, and says the experience made him rethink much of what he had believed about race. He went home with a new name, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz, and a new way of talking about people. What did he see? The Hajj doing what it is built to do. Every pilgrim wears the same simple cloth. Every pilgrim faces the same House. In the rows of prayer, a rich man stands by a poor one and a king could stand by a farmer, heel to heel and shoulder to shoulder. The Qur'an sets human difference beside the sky and the earth: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours." Colors and languages as signs to wonder at, not ranks to climb. A saying reported from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in his farewell sermon makes a similar point: no Arab over a non-Arab, and no one of one color over another, except by mindfulness of God. Malcolm did not live long after. But the letter stayed, and so did the picture: every color, one row.
